shots.text: In a Delhi summer, shade decides whether a street can be walked. GreenCityAI finds the heat, street by street, and tests the fix before anyone builds it.

chapter: A digital twin from open data
shots.text: This is Connaught Place, New Delhi, as a 3D digital twin built only from open data: 212 buildings from OpenStreetMap, 936 trees from a satellite canopy map on AWS Open Data, and the true sun for the fifteenth of May.

Every hour, we trace the sun onto every footpath. At 7 a.m., a third of the walkways are shaded. By noon, the sun is 79 degrees high, and only 4 percent are. The hex map shows where walkers have nowhere to hide.
Around it, we read a kilometre of the city: 658 buildings, 111 junctions, 27 bus stops. And every number wears a label: observed, computed, simulated or proposed.

Pillars mark traffic hot spots from a peak-hour screening model. Analyze scans Middle Circle at Radial Road 2: one approach carries 1.57 times its assumed capacity, and at 3 p.m., 85 percent of nearby walkway is in direct sun.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 is the street doctor. It can only answer by calling our measuring tools, and a checker traces every number it writes back to a tool.
Then we test fixes. Diverting some trips cuts the load from 1.57 to 1.44 times capacity. 200 street trees lift day-long walkway shade from 13.9 to 17 percent. Costs are labelled assumed, not quotes.
It works anywhere in India. Search for Charminar in Hyderabad, and the city map appears at once. Press build, and in about half a minute, a new twin is ready, with its own shade and hot spots.
GreenCityAI: open data in, cooler streets out. Built with AWS Open Data and Claude. The code is on GitHub.
